outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no result has moved the best upper exponent for the planar lattice-point error or settled Hardy's conjecture that the error is O(r^(1/2+eps)); the best exponent I could confirm as unwithdrawn is Li and Yang's 2θ* = 0.628966 (arXiv, August 2023, before the window), and the in-window events are two lower-bound (Omega) refinements of logarithmic factors (Mahatab, April 2025; Lamzouri, May 2026), a numerical study of the conjecture (September 2026, results not read), and papers on variant structures that do not answer the question. No AI system is credited with any event on this problem.
problem_asks: Statement: how far can the number of integer points in a circle centred at the origin be from the circle's area. Unpacked: (1) Upper side: with N(r) the number of integer points (m,n) with m^2+n^2 <= r^2 and E(r) = N(r) - pi r^2, the exponent alpha_0 = inf{alpha : E(r) = O(r^(alpha+eps)) for every eps > 0}, i.e. how large E can be as r grows. (2) Lower side: how large E must be for arbitrarily large r, i.e. the order of E below which it cannot be pushed (the statement's 'how far' also asks for this matching lower bound). (3) Sharpness: whether the upper and lower sides meet, i.e. whether alpha_0 = 1/2 (the conjectured value, E(r) = O(r^(1/2+eps)), against Hardy's lower bound of order r^(1/2)(log r)^(1/4)). Scope: Z^2, the disc centred at the origin, pointwise size of E in the radius r. Mean-square, higher-dimensional, weighted, quasicrystal and hyperbolic analogues are not the question as stated.

events.what_happened: Sierpinski's bound E(R) = O(R^(2/3)) for the circle error, improving Gauss's O(R). The year is given as 1906 by course notes and a 2024 Springer paper, and as 1904 by Cappell and Shaneson (2007), according to search summaries. The original paper was not opened, so this is recorded from secondary sources.
events.delivers: E(R) = O(R^(2/3)) in the radius variable, i.e. exponent 2/3.
events.remains: Every exponent below 2/3, the matching lower bound, and the conjectured exponent 1/2.
events.doubts: Year disputed (1904 vs 1906). Original paper not read.
events.direction: Upper bound, consistent with the conjecture; superseded by later exponents.

events.what_happened: Hardy (1915) and, independently, Landau (1915) proved the lower bound that E(r) is not o(r^(1/2) (log r)^(1/4)), as stated in the live Wikipedia article (opened). This is the Omega side that makes exponent 1/2 a lower bound for any admissible exponent. Their own papers were not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound: |E(r)| is not o(r^(1/2) (log r)^(1/4)) along a sequence of radii, so no admissible exponent is below 1/2. Lower side only.
events.remains: The upper side: whether E(r) = O(r^(1/2+eps)), i.e. whether exponent 1/2 is attained. The best upper exponent is above 1/2 at every date in the record.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjectured exponent 1/2; supplies the lower side.

events.what_happened: Van der Corput (1923) gave an exponent slightly below 2/3 in the radius (below 1/3 in the area variable), per search summaries of Cappell and Shaneson (2007) and course notes. The summaries disagree on whether van der Corput independently obtained the 2/3 bound or refined Sierpinski's. The paper was not opened.
events.delivers: E(R) = O(R^(theta)) for some theta slightly below 2/3, as summarised; the exact value was not verified.
events.remains: Everything below the value obtained and the conjecture.
events.doubts: Exact exponent not verified. Attribution (independent vs refinement) disputed across secondary sources.
events.direction: Upper bound, consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Hafner (1981) proved an Omega-minus lower bound for the circle error, as quoted in Lamzouri (2026, opened): P(x) = Omega-minus((x log x)^(1/4) (log_2 x)^((log 2)/4) exp(-B sqrt(log_3 x))), with x = r^2. The Hafner paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower-bound Omega-minus statement with a log_2 power of about 0.173 and an exp(-B sqrt(log_3 x)) loss.
events.remains: The upper bound; the conjectured exponent; the sharper logarithmic factor now claimed by Lamzouri (2026).
events.direction: Lower bound, consistent with the conjecture.
events.object: Omega-minus lower bound, non-constructive; large values of the error are asserted, not exhibited.

events.what_happened: Iwaniec and Mozzochi, 'On the divisor and circle problems', J. Number Theory 29 (1988) 60-93. Berndt's slide table, as read in search results, gives exponent 7/22 in the area variable X = r^2 (7/11 in the radius) next to this paper. The attribution of that figure to the circle problem (as opposed to the divisor problem) was not confirmed from the paper text.
events.delivers: If the 7/22 figure applies to the circle problem: E(r) = O(r^(7/11+eps)).
events.remains: Everything below 7/11 in radius and the conjecture.

checked_by.qualification: journal of record; referees not named

events.doubts: Circle-problem attribution of the 7/22 exponent not confirmed; paper not opened.
events.direction: Upper bound, consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Huxley's exponent 46/73 for the circle error in the radius (23/73 in the area variable), from 'Exponential sums and lattice points II', as tabulated in search summaries. The year is 1993 in some sources and 1990 in others. Not opened.
events.doubts: Year disputed (1990 vs 1993). Paper not opened.
events.direction: Upper bound, consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Huxley, 'Exponential sums and lattice points III', Proc. London Math. Soc. 87(3) (2003) 591-609, DOI 10.1112/S0024611503014485. The abstract (opened) states that the discrepancy exponent is reduced from 2/3 and 46/73 to 131/208, with a logarithmic factor. Journal online date 23 October 2003; no earlier preprint was found, so the first public argument date is not pinned down beyond the year.
events.revisions: Published online 23 Oct 2003; issue dated Nov 2003. No arXiv preprint found.
events.delivers: E(R) = O(R^(131/208+eps)) with a logarithmic factor; 131/208 ~ 0.629808 (radius).

checked_by.who: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: journal of record; referees not named

events.direction: Upper bound, consistent with the conjecture; the record Li and Yang improve on.

events.what_happened: Soundararajan, 'Omega results for the divisor and circle problems', arXiv math/0302010 (v1, 1 Feb 2003). The abstract (opened) says the paper gives new Omega results for two lattice-point problems and that they are likely the best possible. The circle-problem statement was not read; Mahatab (2025) describes Soundararajan's circle bound as carrying a log_3 factor with power -5/8.
events.delivers: Omega lower-bound results for the circle error with logarithmic factors; exact form and sign not read.
events.remains: The upper exponent; the conjecture; the optimal logarithmic power.
events.doubts: Circle statement not read from the paper; recorded from abstract and from later papers' descriptions.
events.direction: Lower bound, consistent with the conjecture.
events.object: Omega lower bounds with logarithmic factors; non-constructive, not exhibited.

events.what_happened: Cappell and Shaneson, 'Some problems in number theory I: the circle problem', arXiv math/0702613. Versions v1 (21 Feb 2007), v2 (15 Mar 2007), v3 (9 Jul 2007). Per search summaries of the 2014 Shaneson preprint, these versions claimed the conjectured optimal bound O(t^(1/4+eps)) (area variable t, i.e. O(r^(1/2+eps)) in the radius). Version v4 (17 Sep 2014) is withdrawn with the comment 'This paper has been withdrawn as the authors have not succeeded producing an error free version'. The arXiv abstract reads 'This paper concerns the number of lattice points in a circle.' The content of v1-v3 was not read: the ar5iv rendering was empty and the PDF is binary.
events.revisions: v1 21 Feb 2007; v2 15 Mar 2007; v3 9 Jul 2007; v4 17 Sep 2014 withdrawn.
events.delivers: If the summarised claim is what v1-v3 say: E(r) = O(r^(1/2+eps)), the conjectured bound. Withdrawn, and not verified here.
events.remains: As withdrawn, the authors assert nothing; the conjecture is open on the record.
events.time_since_posted: about 19 years (v1); withdrawn about 12 years ago
events.doubts: Withdrawn for lack of an error-free version. The claimed exponent is second-hand (search summary); the content of v1-v3 was not read.

withdrawn.what: Version v4 withdrawn: 'This paper has been withdrawn as the authors have not succeeded producing an error free version'

events.direction: Claimed the conjectured exponent (in favour of the conjecture if correct); withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Bagis, 'On the Solution of Gauss Circle Problem Conjecture', arXiv 1601.02890. Versions v1 (31 Dec 2015) to v6 (5 May 2023). The abstract (opened) gives an asymptotic formula for the mean value of the number of representations of an integer as a sum of two squares. The page carries no withdrawal or journal reference.
events.delivers: An asymptotic for the mean of r(n) over n (a different quantity from the lattice-point error). Does not establish any error exponent for E(r).
events.doubts: The title claims a solution of the conjecture; the abstract concerns the mean of r(n), which is not the error term. Not a resolution of this bullet.
events.direction: Does not bear on the error exponent; recorded as a discounted claim.

events.what_happened: Hulse, Kuan, Lowry-Duda and Walker, 'Second moments in the generalized Gauss circle problem', arXiv 1703.10347 (v1 30 Mar 2017). Dirichlet series and smoothed/sharp sums of P_k(n)^2 for dimensions k >= 3; claims the first power-saving mean-square error term for the dimension-three problem. Opened abstract.
events.delivers: Mean-square and smoothed-sum results in dimension k >= 3, with a dimension-3 mean-square power saving. Nothing pointwise in the planar case.
events.direction: Variant (higher dimension, mean square); does not answer the planar pointwise question.

events.what_happened: Bourgain and Watt, 'Mean square of zeta function, circle problem and divisor problem revisited', arXiv 1709.04340, v1 13 Sep 2017. The circle exponent claimed in this version is 517/824 in the radius (517/1648 in the area variable), as cited second-hand by Lester and Wigman (2023) and a 2024 Springer paper (search summaries; not seen in the abstract, which was cut off). Version v2 (16 Jul 2023), posted by Nigel Watt, is withdrawn. The withdrawal comment (opened) reads: 'A problem with the proofs of Propositions 2 and 3'; 'a similar problem with the proof of Proposition 1'''; 'it is hard to justify the particular application of the Bourgain-Guth reduction theory'; 'Theorems 1, 2 and 3 lose their status as theorems'.
events.revisions: v2 16 Jul 2023: withdrawn by Nigel Watt.
events.delivers: If the withdrawn claims held: E(r) = O(r^(517/824+eps)) in the radius (about 0.6274). Not established: the withdrawal removes Theorems 1-3, and the page does not show which theorem is the circle result.
events.time_since_posted: about 9 years (v1); withdrawn about 3 years 3 months ago
events.doubts: Withdrawn for gaps in Propositions 2, 3 and 1'. Li and Yang (2023) still cite this preprint as [6] several times in Section 5 (for example '[6, Section 7]' and '[6, (6.9)]'). Lester and Wigman (2023) and a 2024 Springer paper, as search summaries report, still call its exponent the current best.

withdrawn.what: Preprint withdrawn; the withdrawal comment says Theorems 1, 2 and 3 'lose their status as theorems' because of gaps in Propositions 2, 3 and 1'

events.direction: Claimed upper bound in favour of the exponent direction; withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Hulse, Kuan, Lowry-Duda and Walker, 'The Laplace transform of the second moment in the Gauss circle problem', arXiv 1705.04771 (v1 12 May 2017; v3 1 Apr 2020). Meromorphic continuation of the Dirichlet series of P_2(n)^2; power-saving improvement on Ivic's Laplace-transform result; main term of order X^(3/2). Opened abstract (partly).
events.delivers: A mean-square (Laplace-transform) asymptotic for P_2(t)^2 in the planar case. Not a pointwise exponent for P_2(t).
events.direction: Variant (mean square); does not bear on the pointwise exponent.

events.what_happened: Lester and Wigman, 'Around the Gauss circle problem: Hardy's conjecture and the distribution of lattice points near circles', arXiv 2305.03549 (v1 5 May 2023; v2 17 May 2023, minor exposition changes; 46 pages). The abstract (opened) examines a folklore random-model heuristic for Hardy's conjecture, shows that autocorrelations of boundary lattice points are determined by a random model, shows that well-separated boundary points behave independently, and formulates a pair-distribution conjecture. No new error bound is claimed in the abstract.
events.delivers: Nothing on the exponent: heuristic and distribution results that support Hardy's conjecture only as heuristics.
events.doubts: No journal publication found. The authors gave talks on the work in 2024 (Mittag-Leffler, Bristol), which show circulation but not verification (search summaries).
events.direction: No bearing on the exponent; heuristic support for the conjectured 1/2.

events.what_happened: Shaneson, 'Estimates on lattice points in the circle', arXiv 1409.2446 (single version, 8 Sep 2014). The abstract (opened) gives an error O(log r * r^(2b)), with b = 5/16 as the simplest estimate (radius exponent 5/8) and the best b = 1507/4875, i.e. radius exponent 3014/4875 ~ 0.618257.
events.revisions: Single version; no later version or journal reference on the page.
events.delivers: Claimed upper bound E(r) = O(r^(0.618257+eps)) (log factor) in the radius. A claimed improvement on Huxley's 131/208; does not reach the conjectured 1/2.
events.remains: The exponent between 1/2 and about 0.618; the conjecture.
events.doubts: Unrefereed single-version preprint. Its author's 2007 claim on the same subject was withdrawn in 2014 (search summary says the 2014 preprint refers to this). No journal venue found. Li and Yang's reference list (read) does not cite it, and the search found no citing paper.
events.direction: Claimed upper bound below Huxley's exponent; does not reach 1/2.

events.what_happened: Kurlberg and Lester, 'Poisson spacing statistics for lattice points on circles', arXiv 2112.08522 (v1 15 Dec 2021). For a density-one set of radii, nearest-neighbour angular spacing of lattice points on circles is Poisson. Search summaries say the paper appeared in Inventiones Mathematicae in 2025 (journal page not opened).
events.revisions: Inventiones Mathematicae 240(2) (2025), per search summary only.
events.delivers: Statement about angular spacing of lattice points on circles, not about the disc error E(r). A neighbouring question.
events.direction: No bearing on the disc error.

events.what_happened: Li and Yang, 'An improvement on Gauss's Circle Problem and Dirichlet's Divisor Problem', arXiv 2308.14859 (v1 28 Aug 2023; v2 14 Sep 2023). Theorem 1.2 (arXiv HTML v2, read): R(X) and Delta(X) are O_eps(X^(theta*+eps)) with theta* = 0.3144831759741... (X = r^2), so E(r) = O(r^(2 theta* + eps)) with 2 theta* = 0.628966... in the radius. The authors compare with 131/416 in X (131/208 in the radius, 0.629807...). The abstract gives no numerical value; it says the gain combines a new first-spacing estimate with Huxley's second-spacing results, and the method is Bombieri-Iwaniec.
events.revisions: v2 14 Sep 2023. No later arXiv version found. Dec 2023 seminar announcement (HIT news, opened) names the same paper. No journal publication found.
events.delivers: Upper bound E(r) = O(r^(0.628966+eps)) in the radius, improving Huxley's 0.629808 by about 0.0009. Does not reach 1/2; the conjecture is untouched. Divisor problem gets the same exponent.
events.remains: The exponent between 1/2 and 0.628966; Hardy's conjecture that exponent 1/2 is attained. (Li and Yang state a conjecture theta = 1/4 in X per search summary; not verified.)
events.doubts: (i) The argument cites Bourgain and Watt, arXiv 1709.04340 (ref. [6]), several times in Section 5. That preprint was withdrawn by its author in July 2023 for gaps in Propositions 2, 3 and 1'. Whether the parts used are the withdrawn ones was not established. (ii) No refereed publication found. (iii) The improvement is marginal. (iv) Its exponent is quoted by later work (Guo, Jiang, Wang and Yang, Dec 2024) without verification.
events.direction: Upper bound improving the record marginally; does not settle the conjecture either way.

events.what_happened: Guo, Jiang, Wang and Yang, 'Bessel functions and Weyl's law for balls and spherical shells', arXiv 2412.14059 (v1 18 Dec 2024). Remark 1.2 (read in HTML v1): '2 theta* = 0.628966..., whereas 131/208 = 0.629807...'; it attributes the improvement to 'Li and the last author in [27]' (Li and Yang). The paper uses that exponent for a Weyl-law remainder on balls and shells in dimensions d >= 2.
events.delivers: Nothing on the planar disc error: it applies Li and Yang's exponent to the Weyl-law remainder for the Dirichlet and Neumann Laplacian on balls. Uptake of the exponent, not verification of it.
events.direction: Not on the problem; a use of the Li-Yang exponent.

events.what_happened: Sourmelidis, 'An additive application of the resonance method', arXiv 2411.14221 (v1 21 Nov 2024). Improves an Omega result of Soundararajan for trigonometric polynomials with positive Fourier coefficients using the resonance method. The abstract (opened) names Dirichlet's divisor problem and Gauss's circle problem as lattice-point applications; no explicit circle exponent was seen.
events.delivers: An Omega-type lower-bound improvement for trigonometric polynomials; the circle-problem consequence is named but not confirmed from what was read.
events.remains: The upper exponent; the conjecture; any circle-specific Omega statement (not verified).
events.doubts: Circle-specific claim not verified. Lamzouri (2026) lists this paper among those it improves.
events.direction: Lower-bound direction, consistent with the conjecture; circle content unverified.

events.what_happened: Edwin and Lin, 'The Gauss Circle Problem and Fourier Quasicrystals', arXiv 2412.05485 (v1 7 Dec 2024). Extends the problem to Fourier quasicrystals; improves the upper bound for uniformly discrete Fourier quasicrystals; for d = 2 gives lower and upper bounds for average error. Opened abstract (partly).
events.delivers: Results on Fourier quasicrystal point sets, not Z^2. Does not change the Z^2 exponent.
events.direction: Variant (quasicrystal); does not answer the question as stated.

events.what_happened: Ehrenborg, 'Gauss Circle Primes', arXiv 2502.06804 (v1 2 Feb 2025). Asks how often the lattice count C(r) in a circle of radius r is prime for r <= n; numerical for n <= 2 x 10^6, with a heuristic. Opened abstract.
events.delivers: Numerical observation and heuristic on primality of lattice counts. No error exponent.
events.direction: Variant (primality of counts); not the error question.

events.what_happened: Mahatab, 'Omega results for the divisor and circle problems using the resonance method', arXiv 2504.17032 (v1 23 Apr 2025 per search summary; v2 3 Sep 2025, read in HTML). Theorem 2 (circle problem, for the sum of r(n) up to X minus pi X): an Omega-type lower bound whose logarithmic factor (log_3 X)^(-3/8) improves Soundararajan's (log_3 X)^(-5/8) (the paper's own words: 'we improve the power from -5/8 to -3/8'). Also Omega bounds for the divisor problem and mean-square zeta results. The sign and full displayed form of Theorem 2 were not confirmed from the portion read.
events.delivers: A lower-bound (Omega) refinement of the logarithmic factor for the circle error. Does not change the upper exponent, so the conjecture is not reached.
events.remains: The upper exponent 0.628966 and the conjectured 1/2.
events.doubts: Theorem 2 read only through the HTML extraction; sign and exact form unconfirmed. Karak (2025) and Lamzouri (2026) describe it as a sharper circle Omega bound.
events.direction: Lower-bound refinement; consistent with the conjectured 1/2.
events.object: Omega-type lower bound for the circle error, obtained by the resonance method; large values asserted, not exhibited.

events.what_happened: Zhao, 'The largest circle enclosing n lattice points', arXiv 2505.06234 (v1 24 Apr 2025; v2 17 May 2025). Elementary plane geometry: n-enclosing circles (interior containing exactly n lattice points); small cases by hand and n < 1100 by computer; conjectures that the set of n admitting such circles is infinite, with infinite complement. Opened abstract.
events.delivers: Nothing on the error term. A neighbouring question about lattice points in discs.
events.direction: Neighbouring question; no bearing.

events.what_happened: Karak, 'Omega estimate for the lattice point discrepancy of a body of revolution using the resonance method', arXiv 2506.22590 (v1 27 Jun 2025). Omega bound for a three-dimensional body of revolution with smooth boundary of bounded nonzero curvature, using Mahatab's resonator; improves Kuhleitner and Nowak. Search summary says published in the Hardy-Ramanujan Journal 48 (2025). Opened abstract page.
events.delivers: Omega result for a 3D body of revolution; not the planar circle.
events.direction: Variant (3D); does not answer the planar question.

events.what_happened: Katsivelos, 'The hyperbolic lattice counting problem in large dimensions', arXiv 2506.17753 (21 June 2025). Average behaviour of the circle-problem error for cocompact lattices acting on hyperbolic space H^n (n >= 3): local averages, quantum variance, spectral exponential sums; Omega results for mean value and second moment. Opened abstract page.
events.delivers: Averaged and Omega results for a hyperbolic analogue. Not the Euclidean disc.
events.direction: Variant (hyperbolic); does not answer the Euclidean question.

events.what_happened: Haynes and Lutsko, 'The Gauss circle problem for Penrose tilings', arXiv 2512.21444 (v1 24 Dec 2025). For unit rhombic Penrose tilings, the number of vertices in a ball of radius R is pi C_P R^2 + O(R^(2/3) (log R)^(2/3)), with C_P ~ 1.231. Opened abstract page.
events.delivers: Error bound for Penrose-tiling vertices, not Z^2. Does not move the Z^2 exponent.
events.direction: Variant (quasicrystal vertex set); does not answer the Z^2 question.

events.what_happened: Gao, 'On the Gauss circle problem over smooth numbers', arXiv 2604.23918 (v1 27 Apr 2026). Asymptotic evaluation of Psi_G(x,y), the sum of r(n) over y-smooth n <= x, in certain ranges. Opened abstract page.
events.delivers: An asymptotic for a smooth-number-weighted sum of r(n). Not the classical disc count; no error exponent in the abstract.
events.direction: Variant (smooth numbers); does not answer the classical question.

events.what_happened: Lamzouri, 'Sharp omega results for the divisor and circle problems', arXiv 2605.21476 (v1 20 May 2026, single version). Theorem 1.1, equation (1.4): for the circle problem, P(x) = Omega-minus((x log x)^(1/4) (log_2 x)^((3/4)(2^(1/3)-1))), with x = r^2, exponent of log_2 about 0.195; the sign is determined. The paper calls the bounds conjecturally sharp (Soundararajan's heuristic; an earlier Lamzouri conjecture), says they improve Soundararajan, Sourmelidis and Mahatab, and gives the first improvement on Hafner's 1981 Omega-minus since. Method: resonance with a one-sided sectorial kernel. Read in the arXiv HTML and abstract.
events.delivers: An Omega-minus lower bound for the circle error: P(x) is not O((x log x)^(1/4) (log_2 x)^(0.195)) in the Omega-minus sense, i.e. a lower-side refinement of the logarithmic factor (in radius, about r^(1/2) (log r)^(1/4) (log log r)^(0.195)). Does not bound the upper side.
events.remains: The upper bound E(r) = O(r^(1/2+eps)) (Hardy's conjecture) and the upper exponent 0.628966.
events.doubts: Sharpness rests on the author's random-model heuristic and an earlier conjecture (stated in the paper). Full proofs not read; only the theorem statement and the acknowledgement were read.
events.direction: Lower-bound refinement; consistent with the conjectured exponent 1/2.
events.object: Omega-minus lower bound for the circle error P(x), x = r^2, from the resonance method. Large values are asserted; no explicit configuration is exhibited.

events.what_happened: Bordignon and Kurlberg, 'Area correlations related to lattice points in discs', arXiv 2607.13659 (v1 15 Jul 2026). Circle flows on tori; an analogue of the Lester-Wigman vanishing area-correlation conjecture is shown to hold in that setting, with densities for the areas in global and local regimes. The abstract (opened) does not state any Gauss-circle error bound.
events.delivers: Results on torus circle flows; no error exponent for the disc count.
events.doubts: A search snippet described a conditional improvement N(R) = pi R^2 + o(R) under a mean-area hypothesis. The abstract page read does not contain that claim, so it is not recorded as a result. Full text not read.
events.direction: Neighbouring analogue; no bearing on the exponent as read.

events.what_happened: Yamaguchi, Fujima, Kuratsubo, Nakai and Yoneda, 'Numerical experiments on the Hardy conjecture for the Gauss circle problem', arXiv 2609.04725 (v1 4 Sep 2026). The abstract (opened) says the paper gives numerical evidence for Hardy's conjecture through large-scale computation. The page comments give 14 pages, 15 figures and 6 FORTRAN programs. The numerical findings were not read.
events.delivers: Numerical evidence only; cannot prove the conjecture. Findings not read.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the conjecture.
events.directly_checkable: Numerical computation of the disc error for large radii (code described, not read).
events.doubts: Numerics support a conjecture; they do not decide it. Results not read.
events.direction: Evidence for Hardy's conjecture; no proof.

disputes.summary: Sierpinski's O(R^(2/3)) bound is dated 1904 by Cappell and Shaneson (2007) and 1906 by course notes and a 2024 Springer paper (search summaries). Van der Corput's role is disputed: Lester and Wigman (2023) credit the 2/3 bound to Voronoi, Sierpinski and van der Corput independently, while Cappell and Shaneson and the course notes treat van der Corput's 1923 result as a refinement.

The Bourgain-Watt exponent (517/824 in the radius, 517/1648 in the area variable) is still cited as the current best by Lester and Wigman (2023) and by a 2024 Springer paper (search summaries), although its author withdrew the preprint in July 2023. Li and Yang (2023) cite the same preprint [6] in their proof.

Sources disagree on the current best exponent. Wikipedia (live, opened) gives 131/208 (Huxley). Guo, Jiang, Wang and Yang (Dec 2024, opened) give 2 theta* = 0.628966 attributed to Li and Yang. Lester and Wigman (2023, search summary) give 1034/1648 (Bourgain-Watt). A UC Davis student report (Spring 2026, search summary; PDF not opened) gives 46/73.
Huxley's 46/73 paper is dated 1990 in some sources and 1993 in others.

Bagis's arXiv paper is titled 'On the Solution of Gauss Circle Problem Conjecture', but its abstract gives an asymptotic for the mean of r(n), not for the lattice-point error. The title claims more than the abstract shows.

A search snippet described Bordignon and Kurlberg (arXiv 2607.13659) as proving a conditional N(R) = pi R^2 + o(R) under a mean-area hypothesis. The abstract page read describes torus circle flows and contains no such result.

summary: Hardy's conjecture (E(r) = O(r^(1/2+eps))) is open at the record date, and the lower bound of order r^(1/2)(log r)^(1/4) is old (Hardy and Landau, 1915). The best upper exponent I could confirm as unwithdrawn is Li and Yang's 2 theta* = 0.628966 in the radius (arXiv 2308.14859, August 2023, Theorem 1.2 read in HTML). It improves Huxley's 131/208 (Proc. LMS 2003, abstract read) by about 0.0009 and predates the window; no refereed publication was found, and it is quoted, not verified, by Guo, Jiang, Wang and Yang (December 2024). Two stronger upper-bound claims are unresolved. Bourgain and Watt (2017) claimed 517/824 in the radius, but the author withdrew the preprint in July 2023 citing gaps in Propositions 2, 3 and 1' and loss of Theorems 1-3 (withdrawal comment read); Li and Yang still cite it several times in their Section 5, and the 2024 Springer paper and Lester and Wigman cite its exponent as current, per search summaries. Shaneson (2014) claims 3014/4875 ~ 0.61826 in the radius, with no journal venue and no citing paper found in the portions I read. Cappell and Shaneson (2007) claimed the conjectured bound and withdrew it in 2014; its content was not read. Within the window, the only events touching the problem's own quantity are lower-bound (Omega) refinements of logarithmic factors: Mahatab (April 2025; log_3 power -3/8 in Theorem 2, read in HTML) and Lamzouri (May 2026; an Omega-minus bound with (log_2 x)^0.195, claimed conjecturally sharp, abstract and theorem statement read). These do not move the upper exponent or settle the conjecture. Other in-window papers are variants (mean square, dimensions three and up, hyperbolic lattices, Penrose vertices, Fourier quasicrystals, smooth-number sums, torus flows, primality of counts) and are recorded as discounted. Yamaguchi et al. (September 2026) offer numerical evidence for the conjecture; their results were not read. Close calls: (a) Li and Yang's exponent is recorded as the best unwithdrawn bound, but its proof leans on the withdrawn Bourgain-Watt preprint, and it was not established whether the parts used are the withdrawn ones; (b) the Mahatab and Lamzouri results change a logarithmic factor on the lower side, and whether a sharper lower-bound log factor counts as movement on 'how far' the error can be is for the later pass; (c) the date of Sierpinski's bound (1904 or 1906) and whether Iwaniec and Mozzochi's 7/22 was a circle-problem result were not resolved from primary text. On AI: no source credits an AI system with any result, proof, idea or check on this problem. Searches of lab announcements, the AlphaEvolve material, Erdos-problem trackers, Tao's blog, science press, and arXiv acknowledgements found nothing on it. The AI-attributed mathematics in the window that I did find concerns other problems: OpenAI's unit-distance counterexample (May 2026; 'an internal OpenAI model', per a blog read in full) and the GPT-counterexample collection by Sra (August 2026, read in the portions that were fetched; none on this problem).
competing_reading: The record can be read as showing no change in the window's upper bound, which is the reading I have taken as the main one. A reader who treats Bourgain-Watt's 517/824 as provisionally valid would name it the record and find it was set before the window (2017); the withdrawal is what removes it. A reader who takes Shaneson (2014) as correct would name 0.61826 as the record, again pre-window and unrefereed. A reader who counts sharper Omega-minus log factors as progress on 'how far' the error can be would call Mahatab (2025) and Lamzouri (2026) advances on the question; I record them as lower-side refinements that leave the upper exponent and the conjecture untouched. A reader who counts Guo, Jiang, Wang and Yang's use of 2 theta* as corroboration of Li and Yang would treat that exponent as more established than I do, since the use is citation, not verification.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report or journal publication for Li and Yang (2023) and for Shaneson (2014), which would show whether either is accepted. (2) The current status of arXiv 1709.04340: the withdrawal comment names Propositions 2, 3 and 1' and Theorems 1-3, but the page did not show which theorem is the circle result, and the full text of Li and Yang's Section 5 would show whether the withdrawn parts are used. (3) The full texts of Lester and Wigman (2023) and of the 2024 Springer paper (not opened), to confirm which Bourgain-Watt exponent each cites and in what form. (4) The v1-v3 text of math/0702613 (Cappell and Shaneson) to confirm what was claimed. (5) Lamzouri's full circle statement and any referee outcome. (6) Any proof of E(r) = O(r^(1/2+eps)), which would settle the conjecture; any proof of a matching upper bound with a sign-definite lower bound would settle it in the form the statement asks.
